newsitem.title: USA: Dole says Clinton has upper hand going into debate.
newsitem.headline: Dole says Clinton has upper hand going into debate.

text.p: Republican presidential candidate Bob Dole on Friday put aside the self-mocking jokes he has been making about his first debate with President Bill Clinton and said he was ready for the Sunday encounter.
But he conceded that Clinton held the advantage.

"I think it's always important to challenge the president. The president always has somewhat of an upper hand. He is the president. He can do things. He can say things," a nervous-sounding Dole told reporters as he took a brief break from dress rehearsals conducted in the ballroom of the ocean-front condominium complex where he has a apartment.

With Tennessee Republican Senator Fred Thompson, a former actor who is playing the role of Clinton in the rehearsals, at his side, Dole added, "It's an opportunity for me, a challenge for me. We think we are ready."

Dole said he recognised the importance of the 90-minute debate in Hartford and conceded he was trailing. "Certainly the president has, apparently has, the lead now. The polls are all over the place. You can't tell," he said.

Dole rehearsed with Thompson for an hour shortly after arriving in Florida on Thursday night and then held a two-hour session with him on Friday morning in the ballroom usually used for weddings and Bar Mitzvahs but now converted into a television studio replica of the room where the two candidates will meet.
Although Dole made a few jokes in his brief encounter with reporters, he sounded nervous. "Ready or not, it's going to happen. It will be very, very interesting. It will be a big challenge for me."

For days, Dole has been making self-mocking jokes about the debate, saying, "If I show up, I will win" and "If I can find Hartford, I'll do alright." But in a comment that reflected deeper feelings, he told a Hartford radio talk show host, Judy Jarvis, on Thursday, "I haven't been so scared for a long time."
Dole and his aides also have been building up President Clinton's powers as a debater in order to lower expectations, a time-honoured political game.

If a candidate isn't expected to do well in a debate and holds his own, then he is often declared the winner. The stakes are high as Dole clearly needs to be impressive to give his floundering campaign a jump start before Election Day on Nov. 5.

The debate is expected to draw a huge television audience -- perhaps akin to the 90 million or more who watch the Super Bowl football championship. "This is the biggest audience I'll ever address, at least for the first few minutes," Dole said earlier in the week.

Not to be outdone, Clinton is playing the same game of lowering expectations as he preps for the debate at a resort in upstate New York. "I'm badly out of shape on this, but I'm trying to get better," Clinton told reporters as he emerged from a lakeside hotel in Chautauqua, N.Y., serving as his pre-debate headquarters.

Some Dole critics charge that his more than a week of preparations have wiped him off the public's radar screen. The only story on Dole in a local paper here on Friday was about a man in the Midwest who robbed a bank wearing a Dole mask and then said, "Don't forget to vote" as he left.
Both inside the party and out, there has been consternation over the generally slow pace of the campaign and at Dole's failure to make inroads against Clinton, as seen in most polls.
Dole seems well aware that time is running out for him to make an impact.

"One of our surveys showed that only 27 percent of the American people are tuned into the presidential race and that there are a lot of people out there who have yet to take note of what's happening," he said in a speech earlier in the week, adding that the debate was "great opportunity" to turn things around.
